elements.label: Early Handheld Electronic Game Without Video Output

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/VideoGame
triples.object: "electronic game involving interaction with a user interface or input device to generate visual feedback from a display device"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/ComputerGameGeneralUsage
triples.object: "'computer game' can be interchangeable with 'video game', especially in the stated regions because of historic domestic microcomputer relevance"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/ComputerGamePCUsage
triples.object: "context distinguishing PC games from console, arcade, and mobile games"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/ComputerGamePCUsage
triples.object: "'computer game' can specifically mean PC game"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/TelevisionGameUsage
triples.object: "1970s and early 1980s; interchangeable with video game in the 1970s"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/TelevisionGameUsage
triples.object: "terms include television game, telegame, and TV game, especially for home consoles connected to a television"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/JapanTVGameUsage
triples.object: "historical usage continuing with TV game into the 21st century"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/JapanTVGameUsage
triples.object: "terms include TV games, TV geemu, and terebi geemu"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/ElectronicGameUsage
triples.object: "electronic game can include video games but also early handheld electronic games lacking video output"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/BusinessWeek1973Article
triples.object: "OED cited this BusinessWeek article as the first printed use"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/Bushnell1972Letter
triples.object: "review of Vending Times and Cashbox suggested the term may appear here earlier; Bushnell used it twice"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/ComputerSpace1971Review
triples.object: "Bushnell believed the term came from a vending-magazine review of Computer Space"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/EdAdlumMarch1973Article
triples.object: "around March 1973 Ed Adlum used the term in an article"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/EarlyVideoGameTermUsage
triples.object: "the first appearance is described as around 1973, while the source discusses documentary evidence from 1971–1973"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/VideoGame
triples.object: "considered to require some interactivity affecting the visual display; this distinguishes limited-interaction interactive films from board games that merely use external media"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/VideoGame
triples.object: "winning conditions such as scoring or a final boss are common but not required; games without them are still commonly justified as video games when the player can interact with a game world"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/VideoGame
triples.object: "common gameplay flow includes title-screen options, levels, avatar control, scoring and power-ups, HUD feedback, health/lives and game-over, bosses, save points/saved games, and in some games a written passage reentered at the title screen"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/CheatMechanism
triples.object: "cheat codes, Easter eggs, and other intentionally hidden secrets can be exploited; cheat cartridges on some consoles execute cheat codes, while user-developed trainers provide similar bypassing for computer games; these may ease the game, add power-ups, or change appearance"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/GamePlatform
triples.object: "specific combination of electronic/computer hardware and associated software; 'system' is also used"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/PlatformExclusivity
triples.object: "platform holders such as Nintendo or Sony may hold multiple brands; games are typically designed for one or a limited number of platforms, and exclusivity to a platform or brand is used as a competitive edge"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/PlatformCategory
triples.object: "traditional categories are arcade, console, and computer; newer expansion includes mobile, virtual/augmented reality, and remote cloud gaming; the source list is explicitly non-exhaustive and excludes capable devices such as PDAs and graphing calculators"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/PortRelease
triples.object: "game developed for an alternative platform than intended; described as a port or conversion"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/RemasterRelease
triples.object: "reuses most original source code while updating art assets, models, and levels for modern systems"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/RemakeRelease
triples.object: "includes asset improvements plus significant reworking of the original game, possibly from scratch"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/PersonalComputerPlatform
triples.object: "not a dedicated game platform, so the same game may run differently on different hardware; openness can allow lower software cost, flexibility, innovation, emulation, mods, and open online hosting"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/HomeConsole
triples.object: "specialized device connected to a television or composite monitor; dedicated hardware gives a concrete target and predictable features, simplifying development versus PC; usually restricts compatible games by platform/company and often comes with a specific controller"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/HandheldConsole
triples.object: "small, portable, self-contained unit with console, screen, speakers and controls; usually less powerful than PC/console hardware; some late-1970s/early-1980s units played one game, 1990s/2000s cartridges enabled many, and handhelds waned in the 2010s as mobile gaming became dominant"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/HandheldConsole
triples.object: "historical changes described from late 1970s through the 2010s"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/ArcadeGameSystem
triples.object: "even more specialized device, typically designed for one game, in a large coin-operated cabinet with built-in console, joystick/buttons, CRT screen, audio amplifier and speakers"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/BrowserGame
triples.object: "uses standardized browser technologies across multiple devices as a cross-platform environment; may be identified by website such as Miniclip or named by programming platform such as Java or Flash"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/MobileGame
triples.object: "on iOS/Android smartphones and tablets may use accelerometers, global-positioning information, and cameras, including for augmented-reality gameplay"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/CloudGamingSession
triples.object: "uses a minimal local device connected to a display with good Internet connectivity; game computation/rendering occurs on provider hardware and predictive methods reduce latency between player input and display output"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/VirtualRealitySystem
triples.object: "generally uses a head-mounted unit with stereoscopic screens and motion tracking responding to head movement; some systems include hand-control units; generally couples to a separate computer, console, or other processing device"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/Emulator
triples.object: "enables games from another system to run in a virtual-machine-like environment on a modern system by simulating original hardware"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/BackwardCompatibility
triples.object: "also allows older games on newer platforms, but typically directly through platform hardware and built-in software"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/DistributionMedium
triples.object: "physical formats include ROM cartridges, magnetic tape/floppy disks, CD-ROM/DVDs, and flash memory cards; Internet/other communications and cloud gaming can remove physical-media need; media may serve as direct read-only game memory or installation media writing main assets to local storage"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/PostReleaseContent
triples.object: "new content and software patches can extend games; expansion packs are typically physical and DLC nominally digital; post-release content may be free or used to monetize the game"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/UserGeneratedContent
triples.object: "players may create content and share it for others to play"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/GameModification
triples.object: "user-created mods alter or add to games, mostly on PCs; they are often unofficial and developed through reverse engineering, while some games provide official modding support"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/GameController
triples.object: "common recent controls include face buttons, shoulder triggers, analog sticks, and d-pads; gamepads/joysticks are common for consoles and PC accessories, while PCs also use keyboard and mouse"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/StandardController
triples.object: "typically bundled with consoles; similar control sets are integrated in handheld consoles and arcade cabinets"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/PeripheralController
triples.object: "available separately from console makers or third parties"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/SpecializedController
triples.object: "examples include racing wheels, light guns and dance pads for particular genres"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/SensorInput
triples.object: "touchscreens/motion sensors broaden interaction; cameras, microphones and motion detectors capture player sound/movement and can enhance VR immersion"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/VisualOutputForm
triples.object: "video games are intended to output graphics to video displays including CRT/LCD televisions, built-in screens, projectors or computer monitors; forms range from fixed LED/LCD and text-based displays through 2D/3D graphics and augmented-reality displays"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/VisualPerformanceFeature
triples.object: "color depth, refresh rate, frame rate and screen resolution are jointly determined by game-platform limitations, display-device limitations and program efficiency"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/AudioElement
triples.object: "graphics are often accompanied by sound through internal platform speakers or external speakers; sound effects can be tied to player actions for audio feedback, with background music also present"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/HapticTechnology
triples.object: "commonly built into a controller; controller shaking can simulate an in-game earthquake and provide extra player feedback"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/GameGenre
triples.object: "generally based on gameplay interaction rather than narrative setting; horror is an identified exception based on horror-fiction, supernatural and psychological-horror narrative elements"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/GTACloneGenre
triples.object: "Grand Theft Auto clone from Grand Theft Auto III"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/BattleRoyaleGenre
triples.object: "battle royale from the film Battle Royale"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/FirstPersonShooterGenre
triples.object: "originally called 'Doom clones' based on the 1993 game; genre names can shift as players, developers and media introduce new terms"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/GameGenre
triples.object: "hierarchy includes broad top-level genres such as shooter/action, subgenres such as first- and third-person shooter, and cross-genre types such as action-adventure that fall under multiple top-level genres"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/MultiplayerMode
triples.object: "multiplayer can be local on one device, on separate devices over a local network such as a LAN party, or online via separate Internet connections"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/MultiplayerConfiguration
triples.object: "most multiplayer games are competitive; many offer cooperative, team-based and asymmetric options"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/MassivelyMultiplayerOnlineGame
triples.object: "online server structures can support MMOs with hundreds of players at the same time"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/ZeroPlayerGame
triples.object: "small set of games with very limited interaction, commonly simulations where the player may set a starting state and then watch as a passive observer"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/CoreGame
triples.object: "typically requires substantial time to learn/master and appeals mainly to gamers rather than a broader audience"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/CasualGame
triples.object: "designed for accessibility, simple gameplay and quick rules, aimed at a mass market, and often supports jumping in and out on demand"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/HyperCasualGame
triples.object: "even more simplistic rules for short but infinitely replayable games; Flappy Bird is the example"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/EdutainmentGame
triples.object: "tends to focus on entertainment and rote learning and is unlikely to engage critical thinking"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/EducationalVideoGame
triples.object: "geared toward problem solving through motivation and positive reinforcement while downplaying entertainment value"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/SeriousGame
triples.object: "non-entertainment purposes may augment, overshadow or eliminate entertainment; educational games are serious games; other types include fitness games (physical exercise), simulator games (e.g. piloting aircraft), advergames (product advertising), and newsgames (advocacy messages)"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/ArtGame
triples.object: "developed to communicate a story/message as art; designed to generate emotion/empathy, challenge societal norms and critique through interactivity; may lack a win condition and is designed for exploration"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/ContentRating
triples.object: "identifies a target age group; nearly all systems use a minimum-age identifier plus descriptors; review commonly considers violence type/graphicness and sexual content, and may identify drug/alcohol use and gambling"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/ESRB
triples.object: "ratings are voluntary; E Everyone, E10+ Everyone 10+, T Teen, M Mature, AO Adults Only"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/PEGI
triples.object: "United Kingdom, most of the European Union, and other European countries"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/PEGI
triples.object: "replaces earlier national-based systems in stated coverage; source lists minimum recommended ages 3+, 8+, 12+, 16+, 18+"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/ACB
triples.object: "ratings G, PG, M, MA15+, R18+, X; can issue RC Refused Classification; ratings are enforceable by law and unrated/RC games cannot be imported or purchased digitally in Australia"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/CERO
triples.object: "A all ages, B 12+, C 15+, D 17+, Z 18+"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/IARC
triples.object: "created by major rating providers to streamline/align regions so a publisher can complete one provider review and use the IARC transition to affirm ratings in other regions"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/GermanyPre2018NaziImageryPolicy
triples.object: "USK would refuse to classify games depicting Nazi imagery; the source then says 'and thus allow sale', an internal inconsistency preserved here; developers often replaced such imagery with fictional imagery"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/GermanyPost2018SocialAdequacyPolicy
triples.object: "ruling relaxed to allow Nazi imagery for 'social adequacy' purposes applied to other artworks"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/ChinaGamePublicationReview
triples.object: "all published games must pass strict government review; content such as smearing the image of the Chinese Communist Party is disallowed; foreign games often require developer/publisher modification"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/EarlyVideoGamePrototypes
triples.object: "simple extensions of electronic games using video-like output from room-sized mainframes"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/Spacewar
triples.object: "earlier computer game that inspired Computer Space"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/ArcadeGoldenAge
triples.object: "rapid arcade-era growth; Atari, Mattel and Coleco released successful home consoles"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/NorthAmericanMarketCrash1983
triples.object: "loss of publishing control and console-market saturation led to the North American crash"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/Late1980sConsoleShift
triples.object: "by the late 1980s consoles were dominated by Japanese companies such as Nintendo, Sega and later Sony"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/PCDominanceShift
triples.object: "Microsoft Windows, with MS-DOS before it, increasingly dominated computer gaming; multiplayer online PC games saw a nascent eSports scene"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/ArcadeAndHandheldShift
triples.object: "arcades lost technological edge/popularity by the end of the 1990s, especially in North America/Europe; Nintendo dominated handhelds with Game Boy"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/BigThreeConsoleEra
triples.object: "by the 2000s Sega exited consoles; Nintendo, Sony and Microsoft became the 'big three'"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/AAACentering
triples.object: "core industry increasingly centered on AAA games, reducing room for riskier experimental lower-budget games"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/IndieRise
triples.object: "high-speed Internet and digital distribution enabled indie development to gain prominence into the 2010s"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/SmartphoneAndAsianMarketShift
triples.object: "emerging Asian markets and smartphone proliferation shifted demographics toward casual/cozy gaming and increased monetization via games as a service"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/GlobalVideoGameMarket2020
triples.object: "estimated annual revenue in 2020 was US$159 billion across hardware, software and services; stated as three times the global music industry and four times the film industry in 2019"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/IndustryParty
triples.object: "developers, publishers, distributors, retailers, hardware manufacturers and other marketers liaise to bring games to consumers"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/HardwareDesignInnovation
triples.object: "PC-component, console and peripheral sales plus demand for better game performance are powerful drivers of hardware design and innovation in the electronics industry"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/OnlineMultiplayerMode
triples.object: "multiplayer can occur online via separate Internet connections; online server structures can enable MMOs with hundreds of players at the same time"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/Esports
triples.object: "multiplayer online PC games saw the establishment of a nascent eSports scene"

triples.subject: https://example.org/ontology/video-game/GamesAsAService
triples.object: "incorporating games as a service is described as increasing monetization amid smartphone-game proliferation and changing player demographics"
